properties.note: Hand-curated reference documents tied to a place, shown as a map marker you click for a popup — the full text lives here so it works fully offline, no link-out required. Started with geology, then history (subdivided by era), demographics (structured population/age data instead of prose — see the 'demographics' property and _formatDemographics in app.js), and island-info (ownership/access/land-trust/Maine-Island-Trail status — see the 'islandInfo' property and _formatIslandInfo); category field is deliberately generic so this can extend further later (flora/fauna, etc). Add entries as sources are found — see AudioChart session notes for sourcing conventions. Demographics figures are individually dated to their real census year (2020 population; age data is 2010 Census where that's the most recent published for a given small town) rather than implying more current data than exists; seasonal summer/winter contrast is included only where a real source documents something concrete, never fabricated. Island-info entries source ownership/access from Maine Coast Heritage Trust preserve pages, NPS, and Wikipedia; onMaineIslandTrail is null (not true/false) when no source confirms or denies MITA status one way or the other — never assumed. Maine reuses island names constantly (multiple Bear Islands, Green Islands, Crow Islands, Sheep Islands, Stave Islands, etc. across different bays) — every island-info `title` therefore carries a disambiguating "(Locality)" suffix, e.g. "Bear Island (Eggemoggin Reach)" / "Bear Island (Northeast Harbor)", "Crow Island (Cranberry Isles)", so the popup header alone is never ambiguous. Apply this to every new island-info entry, not just ones with a known collision — the locality is usually the town or named archipelago from the `place` field. See _bareIslandName() in app.js, which strips this suffix back off before matching against the chart data's own (bare-named) island list for the click-for-name dot layer.

properties.title: The Cranberry Island Series
properties.body:
The Cranberry Isles and the southwestern part of Mount Desert Island are built largely from volcanic eruptions that took place along this stretch of coast about 380-400 million years ago — dated more precisely, at one location, to 378 million years by radiometric methods. Geologists split the rock into three types: felsites and volcanic flows, volcanic tuffs, and interbedded volcanic and sedimentary rock. It's generally light gray or blue-gray, most easily recognized by its layers of tuff — rock built from small fragments of volcanic debris that settled after an explosive eruption.

The rock has been folded to some degree, but — worth being precise about, since it's easy to assume otherwise — the Maine Geological Survey's own account is explicit that it does NOT show strong metamorphism, unlike the older Ellsworth Schist found elsewhere on Mount Desert Island, which was buried, heated, and squeezed into true metamorphic rock. The Cranberry Island Series is volcanic through and through, but not metamorphosed.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Bulletin 38 — The Geology of Mount Desert Island

properties.title: Volcanic tuff, west shore
properties.body: Extensive exposures of volcanic tuff line the west shore — angular fragments of volcanic debris, from a fraction of an inch to a few inches across, cemented together after an explosive eruption. The island's southern end tells a different story: layered sedimentary rock with only occasional tuff beds, part of the same Cranberry Island Series but laid down more quietly between eruptions.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Bulletin 38 — The Geology of Mount Desert Island

properties.title: Old lava flows, north-side ledges
properties.body: The ledges on the island's north side expose rock thought to be old lava flows. Its chaotic, jumbled appearance comes from the lava continuing to move while it cooled and solidified — solid blocks of already-hardened rock got caught up and engulfed in the still-molten lava around them, which then crystallized in place, blocks and all.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Bulletin 38 — The Geology of Mount Desert Island

properties.title: Volcanic tuff, Seawall picnic area
properties.body: A well-known, easy-to-reach exposure of volcanic tuff — part of the same Cranberry Island Series found across the strait on the Cranberry Isles themselves. Look closely at the rock in front of the picnic-ground parking area and you'll see a variety of angular fragments, from a fraction of an inch up to a few inches across, all cemented together after an explosive volcanic eruption roughly 380-400 million years ago.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Bulletin 38 — The Geology of Mount Desert Island

properties.title: Ancient Volcanic Rocks of the Vinalhaven Rhyolite
properties.body:
Vinalhaven splits into two very different stories. The central and southern part of the island is a massive body of pink granite — the famous Vinalhaven granite, quarried through the late 1800s and early 1900s for dimension stone and decorative work on buildings and bridges in Boston, New York, and Chicago. The old quarries are inactive now.

The northern part, from Middle Mountain to Browns Head, is a suite of volcanic rocks called the Vinalhaven Rhyolite — arguably more interesting, if less famous. It records an ancient volcano: flow-banded rhyolite (a hard, striped rock formed as thick, taffy-like lava was stretched moving up the vent), volcanic breccia (angular fragments blown apart in explosive eruptions), water-laid tuff (volcanic debris sorted into layers by water washing it downslope), and even rare accretionary lapilli — small round "mud balls" that form when fine volcanic ash mixes with rain inside an eruption cloud and grows in layers like a hailstone before falling to the ground. The Maine Geological Survey compares the volcanic activity that produced these rocks to what's active today in the Caribbean or the Aegean Sea. Best estimate for its age: Silurian, more than 420 million years old.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Ancient Volcanic Rocks on Vinalhaven Island (1998)

properties.title: Supervolcano-scale eruptions at Western Head
properties.body:
Most of Isle au Haut sits on granite and gabbro — igneous rock that cooled slowly underground, dated to about 424 million years old. But the western shore, especially Western Head, exposes something rarer: the actual explosive-eruption deposits themselves, more than 3 kilometers thick in places, among the most spectacular examples of this age anywhere on the Maine coast (others include Vinalhaven, Swans Island, Mount Desert Island, and the Cranberry Isles).

The cliffs there show the full range of pyroclastic rock — deposits of fragments blown apart by violent eruptions, from fine ash to lapilli to house-sized blocks. Look for tuff-breccia, welded layers with flame-shaped "fiamme" (flattened pumice fragments), and layering that shows the eruptions came in a rapid series, not one single event. Recent research suggests this was a continental-margin volcanic arc above a subduction zone, part of a chain dramatic enough that some of the eruptions may have reached true supervolcano scale — though with only fragments of the record preserved, that's hard to prove outright.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Beautifully Preserved Volcanic Debris in Bedrock, Western Head, Isle au Haut (2015)

properties.title: The Battie Quartzite
properties.body:
Mount Battie's famous view over Camden and Penobscot Bay exists because of what's underfoot: the Battie Quartzite, a metamorphic rock hard enough to resist the erosion that wore down everything around it, leaving the mountain standing above its surroundings. The rock began, over 500 million years ago in the Cambrian, as sand and pebbles accumulating on the floor of the Iapetus Ocean — the long-vanished predecessor to the Atlantic — near what was then the south margin of that ocean, not far from the South Pole.

Remarkably, the original sedimentary story survived the metamorphism that hardened it into quartzite around 430 million years ago in the Silurian. Near the summit and down the south side, you can still see the original pebbles as white shapes in the gray rock — a conglomerate, the metamorphosed remains of an ancient pebble beach or channel deposit. Further north and east the rock is mostly bedded quartzite (metamorphosed sand layers), some with cross-lamination showing the sand was rippled by currents before the next layer buried it. The mountain's modern shape is much younger still — the last continental ice sheet finished sculpting it only about 14,000 years ago.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — The Bedrock Geology of Mount Battie, Camden (2001)

properties.title: The Megunticook Formation along Bald Mountain
properties.body: The rocks along the Bald Mountain Trail belong to the Megunticook Formation, and like Mount Battie's quartzite nearby, they began as ordinary sediment — quartz-rich sandstone and mudstone — accumulating in an ocean basin over 500 million years ago in the Cambrian. In places the trail still shows recognizable sandstone beds; elsewhere the rock was originally just plain mudstone. These rocks were pushed to a notably high metamorphic grade, probably during the Silurian around 420 million years ago — more intensely altered than many of their neighbors along the coast.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Glimpses of Geologic History along the Bald Mountain Trail, Camden (2020)

properties.title: The Spruce Head granite pluton
properties.body: The white bedrock along this stretch of coast, and on Ash Island just offshore, is part of the Spruce Head pluton — once a large mass of molten rock that cooled and crystallized deep underground about 421 million years ago (give or take a million), later brought back up to the surface by millions of years of uplift and erosion. The same pluton reaches Clark Island a few miles south, where a different zone of it was quarried commercially for a century.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Birch Point Beach State Park, Owls Head (2009)

properties.title: Granite, quarries, and an immigrant village
properties.body:
Clark Island sits on the same Spruce Head Pluton as Birch Point up the coast, dated to about 421 million years old, late in the Silurian. The island's north end (public) is muscovite-biotite-garnet granodiorite and granite; the south end (private) is a different zone entirely — quartz gabbro, quartz diorite, tonalite.

The real story here, though, is what people did with the rock. The Clark Island — or Hocking — granite quarry opened around 1870 and grew into a serious industrial operation: a pit eventually 500 by 300 feet and 50 feet deep, 8 derricks, a full stone-cutting plant, and an entire company village with its own post office. Immigrant stonecutters from Sweden, Finland, Scotland, and England lived and worked on the island. The larger quarry pit is now a brackish, spring-fed swimming hole, its walls still showing glacial polish and striations from the ice sheet that scraped over this coast at the end of the last Ice Age.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Clark Island Preserve, St. George (2024)

properties.title: The Islesboro Formation
properties.body: The bedrock at Grindle Point, on northern Penobscot Bay's island of Islesboro, belongs to the Islesboro Formation — metamorphic rock whose original sediment is thought to be Cambrian or even late Precambrian in age, over 500 million years old. Exactly when it was metamorphosed and faulted isn't as well pinned down, but it's probably Silurian. Thin, dark green igneous dikes cut across the formation in many places on the island — later intrusions of molten rock into cracks in the already-solid metamorphic rock.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Grindle Point, Islesboro (2007)

properties.title: Two volcanoes, one collision, one ocean opening
properties.body:
Harriman Point, on the west side of Blue Hill Bay, preserves an unusually complete geologic story. Around 500 million years ago, sediment eroded from nearby land settled here on an ocean floor alongside material from two very different kinds of volcanoes — silica-poor ones like today's Mount Rainier or Mount St. Helens, producing basalt, and their silica-rich counterparts.

By about 430 million years ago these layers had been buried, heated, and deformed as part of the larger Appalachian mountain-building event, altering their original minerals into metamorphic rock. Much later, starting around 250 million years ago, the supercontinent Pangea began breaking apart and the North Atlantic Ocean started to open; the cracks that formed as the continents pulled away filled with basaltic rock, now solidified into the dark dikes you can still find cutting through the older rock here. After the mountains rose and eroded for some 400 million years, the last Ice Age's ice sheets — beginning about 100,000 years ago — gave the point its present shape.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Bedrock, Glaciers, and People at Harriman Point, Brooklin (2022)

properties.title: A sliver of Earth's mantle
properties.body:
Pine Hill is a small, unassuming 100-foot knob with one of the strangest rocks anywhere in Maine underfoot: serpentinized peridotite. Peridotite is what Earth's mantle itself is thought to be made of — dense, low-silica, iron- and magnesium-rich rock, quite unlike the granites and volcanics that make up most of the surrounding coast. Here, heat, pressure, and water have converted most of its original olivine into dark green serpentine, giving the rock a distinctive waxy sheen where aligned serpentine plates catch the light.

How a piece of the mantle ended up exposed on a small Penobscot Bay hilltop is still genuinely debated: it may have risen as magma from great depth, or it could be a sliver of ancient oceanic crust thrust up onto the continent when tectonic plates collided. Either way, the rock's unusual chemistry — low in silica, high in iron and magnesium, low in calcium — supports some of the rarest plant species found anywhere in the state.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Pine Hill Serpentinized Peridotite, Little Deer Isle (2016)

properties.title: Lime kilns and glacial grooves
properties.body:
Rockport sits on the same belt of limestone that runs through Rockland and Camden, and for most of the 1800s that limestone was the town's economic engine: quarried nearby (notably at what's now the Simonton Corner Quarry Preserve), then burned in kilns at the harbor to produce lime for mortar and building. The ruins of several old stone lime kilns still stand at the harbor park today.

The bedrock itself carries an older story too — folded limestone with harder, silica-rich mineral veins running parallel to the fold axis, formed as the rock deformed. And on some of the exposed ledges near the harbor, you can find two sets of glacial grooves gouged directly into the limestone, cut by the ice sheet as it dragged rock debris across the surface during the last Ice Age.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Rockin' around Rockport Harbor (2009)

properties.title: The Deer Isle granite pluton
properties.body: Most of Deer Isle — including the town of Stonington and many of the smaller islands scattered south and east of it — sits on a single large body of granite known as the Deer Isle pluton, dated to about 371 million years old in the Devonian Period. For two centuries this granite was a major industry, quarried from multiple sites across the pluton and shipped out to build much of the eastern seaboard. Settlement Quarry itself, on Oceanville Road, has been inactive for decades; the Island Heritage Trust now maintains it as a preserve with walking trails and signage explaining both the geology and the quarrying history on site.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Settlement Quarry, Stonington (2011)

properties.title: A microcontinent collision, folded into stone
properties.body: The rock at the old Thomaston Prison Quarry spans a huge stretch of time — metamorphic rock ranging from Precambrian (possibly as old as 650 million years) to Ordovician (as young as roughly 450 million years). Both age groups were caught up together in the same event around 400 million years ago, the Devonian: the Acadian orogeny, when a microcontinent called Avalon collided with North America and shoved regional thrust sheets of rock into place. That collision is why folding and faulting shows up in coastal Maine bedrock so widely — and it's on vivid display in the quarry itself, where small, tight folds (geologists nickname them Z-folds and S-folds, after the letter shapes they trace) record the rock bending under that pressure.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Thomaston Prison Quarry, Thomaston (2002)

properties.title: A submarine canyon was the ancestral Penobscot River
properties.place: Penobscot Bay, West Passage (Owls Head to Vinalhaven)
properties.body:
The bay itself has a story worth knowing. Southeast of Rockland, in the West Passage, the sea floor drops into a real canyon — over 500 feet deep at one spot between Owls Head and Vinalhaven, visible on ordinary nautical charts if you know to look. It isn't a fluke of erosion by today's currents: it's the drowned channel of the Penobscot River itself.

At the peak of the last Ice Age, roughly 20,000 years ago, the weight of the ice sheet pressed the land down into the mantle. As the ice melted, the land sprang back up faster than the ocean could refill — dropping relative sea level as much as 180 feet below today's, between about 11,000 and 10,000 years ago. At that low stand, this canyon was dry land: the Penobscot River's own gorge, opening into the sea about seven nautical miles south of modern Vinalhaven. Matinicus was a mountaintop on the mainland. Vinalhaven and North Haven were joined into one long peninsula reaching all the way from Castine and Cape Rosier. A large tidal bay, something like today's Great Bay in New Hampshire, sat just east of Rockland — ten nautical miles long, with the modern Rockland waterfront about 2.5 miles inland from its shore. As the Gulf of Maine keeps rising, the coast keeps changing still.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Penobscot Bay 10,000 Years Ago: A Submarine Canyon Was the Ancestral Penobscot River Valley (1999)

properties.title: The 1996 Rockland landslide
properties.body:
In the early hours of April 16, 1996, a 50-foot bluff on the north shore of Rockland Harbor gave way. Most of the initial slumping happened between 1:15 and 4:00 AM on a falling tide, before any heavy rain — this wasn't simple rain-triggered erosion. Portions of two houses, built about 75 feet back from the bluff edge, collapsed into the slide. Within a week the failure had displaced more than half an acre of the original bluff top, moved material over 400 feet out onto the intertidal mudflats, and disturbed 3.5 acres in total. Smaller blocks kept calving off the scarp for a month afterward.

The underlying cause: the bluff was built on soft glacial-marine clay, the kind of unstable coastal material found in bluffs up and down this part of the Maine coast. The city, with partial FEMA funding, stabilized the site with a sequenced fill — heavy rock riprap at the toe, progressively lighter cement-kiln dust higher up the slope — then capped it with topsoil and grass. No lives were lost, but the two homes were a total loss and the stabilization project alone ran over $750,000. It's a dramatic example of a slow, ongoing process along much of the Maine coast: marine bluffs built on this kind of soft glacial clay erode, sometimes catastrophically.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Aftermath of the 1996 Rockland Landslide (1997)

properties.title: Possibly the largest pockmarks in the world
properties.body:
The muddy floor of Belfast Bay is pitted with more than 2,000 crater-like depressions called pockmarks — and some of them, up to 350 meters across and 50 meters deep, are possibly the largest such features found anywhere on Earth. They're not volcanic or impact craters: they're where methane gas, trapped in the mud beneath the seabed, has erupted upward and blown a hole in the sea floor.

Most pockmarks elsewhere in the world form over petroleum deposits, where high-temperature breakdown of oil generates the gas. That's not what's happening here — the bedrock under Belfast Bay is metamorphic and igneous rock that never got hot enough to form oil and gas in the first place. Instead, the methane here is biological: ordinary bacteria breaking down organic matter in mud less than 10,000 years old, the same process that happens in any muddy seabed. What's unusual isn't the methane — it's the sheer size of the pockmark field it produced. Similar, smaller pockmark fields exist in Blue Hill Bay, Oak Bay, and Eggemoggin Reach.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Belfast Bay Pockmark Field (1997)

properties.title: Slump-folded mud beneath the lighthouse
properties.body:
The rock exposed around Marshall Point Light — the lighthouse made famous by its long walkway, familiar from film — is metamorphic rock of the Benner Hill sequence, originally ordinary sediment deposited in an ocean basin around 440-500 million years ago in the Ordovician. Before it ever hardened into rock, some of those layers of sand and mud slumped down an underwater slope and got folded and contorted while still soft — a shape later locked in permanently as heat and pressure from mountain-building, and nearby intrusions of molten rock between about 440 and 360 million years ago, metamorphosed and further deformed the layers.

Look for the dikes too: younger igneous rock, probably Silurian (~420 million years old), cuts straight across the older metamorphic rock in visible streaks. In places you can see gray granite and dark basalt mingled together in the same dike, with scalloped, interlocking edges — evidence that two different molten rocks were both liquid at once and interacted without fully mixing, the basalt solidifying first because it cools at a higher temperature than granite.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Marshall Point Lighthouse and Geology, Port Clyde (2000)

properties.title: Glacial striations and the Ice Age's last mile
properties.body:
The bedrock along the Moose Point shoreline is metamorphic rock of the Penobscot Formation, roughly 490 million years old — but the far more recent story here is written on top of it. Rub a pencil across the right patch of weathered ledge and you can reveal glacial striations: scratch marks gouged into the rock as the ice sheet dragged embedded rock debris across it, still pointing south-southeast, the exact direction that ice was flowing between about 30,000 and 15,000 years ago.

Dig a little and you'll find glacial till near the park entrance — unsorted rubble dropped directly by the ice — with individual stones still showing their own transport striations. And along the shoreline, layered silt and clay sits right on top of the till: sediment that settled quietly to the floor of the ocean during the marine submergence that followed the ice sheet's retreat, when the weight of the ice was gone but the crust hadn't yet sprung back up.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Geologic Site of the Month — Glacial Geology of Moose Point State Park, Searsport (2013)

properties.title: The Penobscot Formation and a glacial beach
properties.body:
Sears Island — 937 acres, largely under conservation easement, laced with trails open to non-motorized recreation — is underlain entirely by the Penobscot Formation, a dark gray schist that weathers rusty-brown. It began as fine silty mud on the slope of an ancient ocean-arc system, probably in the late Cambrian to early Ordovician, before a Silurian-age collision between island arcs folded and metamorphosed it into the sheet-like, foliated schist you can see in outcrop along the shore.

The beach tells a different, much more recent story: boulders and cobbles of rock types that don't match the island's own bedrock at all — granite flecked with feldspar and mica, banded gneiss, garnet-bearing schist — rounded either by glacial transport or by the modern waves. They're erratics, carried here from elsewhere by the ice sheet (or reworked since by the surf) and dropped on an island whose own foundation is a single, uniform formation.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — Sears Island, Searsport (2018)

properties.title: Five rock formations along the old rail bed
properties.body: The 2.2-mile Passagassawakeag ('Passy') Rail Trail, laid on a former railroad bed along the river of the same name, happens to cross five distinct bedrock formations in one short walk — the Bucksport Formation, Appleton Ridge Formation, Ghent Phyllite, an unnamed quartz-rich metasiltstone, and the Gushee member of the Penobscot Formation, running roughly northeast to southwest. The trail's northern half sits on the Bucksport Formation specifically: metasedimentary rock that started as ordinary marine sand and calcareous mud, and was later metamorphosed into 'granofels' — a fine-grained, granular rock built from quartz, feldspar, and (in its sandier layers) biotite mica. Large outcrops of it are visible right along the trail, alongside smaller exposures of the neighboring Appleton Ridge Formation.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Geologic Facts and Localities — The Passagassawakeag Rail Trail, Belfast (2017)

properties.title: Champlain sails into the bay
properties.body: In September 1604, Samuel de Champlain — part of the first permanent French attempt at a colony in the region, at St. Croix Island that same year — sailed into the Penobscot River with Wabanaki guides who had been helping him read the coast all summer. Here he met and conferred with Bashaba, the sachem the French recorded as principal chief along this river, in one of the earliest documented encounters between Europeans and the Wabanaki people of this exact bay. Champlain pushed on upriver as far as present-day Bangor, hunting for a passage inland and for Norumbega, the legendary city of gold that turned out not to exist. What he did produce, over that summer and the following years exploring the Maine and Massachusetts coast, were among the first accurate charts of this coastline based on real, firsthand survey — work this app's own charts trace their lineage back to, four centuries later.
properties.source: University of Maine Canadian-American Center; Maine Memory Network — Champlain and the Settlement of Acadia, 1604-1607

properties.title: Fort Pownall, built to hold the frontier
properties.place: Fort Point State Park, Stockton Springs
properties.body:
In May 1759, during the French and Indian War, 400 men sailed up from Newbury, Massachusetts and built a fort here in a matter of weeks — Massachusetts Governor Thomas Pownall's answer to French and Native resistance further up the Penobscot. Ninety-foot palisaded walls surrounded a moat fifteen feet wide, with a two-story, forty-four-foot blockhouse at the center and diamond-shaped riflemen's flankers at each corner, reached by drawbridge. It was meant to plug the river and make the area safe for English settlement, pushing back the Penobscot and Norridgewock peoples who had long used this water.

The fort never fired a shot in anger during the war it was built for. Its real moment came at the start of a different war: in 1775, with the Revolution just breaking out, British forces confiscated its guns and ammunition — and a Continental Army colonel named Cargill burned the fort to the ground and filled in its moat himself, rather than let the British hold it. Only earthworks remain today at Fort Point State Park, at the tip of Cape Jellison where it juts into the bay.
properties.source: Maine Historic Preservation Commission — Fort Pownall, 1759, Stockton Springs, Waldo County

properties.title: The Penobscot Expedition — America's forgotten naval disaster
properties.body:
In June 1779 the British landed about 750 troops on the peninsula where the Bagaduce and Penobscot Rivers meet and began building Fort George — a Loyalist haven, a source of Royal Navy timber, and a naval base to threaten New England's coast. Massachusetts responded with the largest American naval expedition of the whole Revolutionary War: 19 armed vessels and 24 transports, over 1,000 militia, commanded by Commodore Dudley Saltonstall at sea and Brigadier General Solomon Lovell ashore — with the artillery under a lieutenant colonel named Paul Revere.

The siege dragged on for three weeks without Saltonstall pressing the naval attack he had the firepower to win. On August 13, a British relief fleet of seven warships under Sir George Collier arrived. Rather than fight through them, Saltonstall retreated up the Penobscot River — and the entire American fleet was scuttled or burned by its own crews rather than let it fall into British hands. Forty-two of 44 ships were lost, 474 men killed, wounded, captured, or missing: the worst defeat in American naval history until Pearl Harbor, 162 years later. Saltonstall was court-martialed and dismissed from the service; Paul Revere, also court-martialed over his conduct in the retreat, was eventually acquitted.
properties.source: Castine Historical Society; American Battlefield Trust — Penobscot Expedition, 1779

properties.title: The island town that vanished overnight
properties.body:
Civil War veteran Davis Tilson bought Hurricane Island in 1870 and built a granite-quarrying operation that, at its 1880s-1900s peak, supported a company town of up to 1,200 people — a Catholic church, a school, a company store, and a genuinely international workforce of Swedish, Finnish, Irish, Scottish, English, and Italian stonecutters and carvers. Granite carved in its sheds went into the Brooklyn Bridge, the Washington Monument, post offices in Baltimore and Pittsburgh, even cobblestones in Havana.

It ended almost as suddenly as it began. By the 1910s reinforced concrete was replacing granite as the building material of choice nationwide, and in 1914 — not long after a shipment of Hurricane Island granite sank en route to Rockland Harbor and the company's foreman died unexpectedly — the operation simply stopped. Management told the townspeople to leave, provided a few boats, and gave them barely any time to do it. Families who had lived their whole lives on the island abandoned their homes almost overnight. The island today is a field station; walk it and you can still find the quarry pits, building foundations, and the bones of the town that disappeared.
properties.source: Hurricane Island Center for Science and Leadership; Wikipedia — Hurricane Island (Maine)

properties.title: One-tenth of America's deep-water captains
properties.body:
For a stretch of the 19th century, this one small Penobscot Bay town produced roughly a tenth of all deep-water sea captains sailing under the American flag — more per square mile than anywhere else in the country, by some counts around 300 commanders in all. It wasn't incidental: captaincy ran in families here, passed from father to son for generations, and at its shipbuilding peak Searsport ran 17 shipyards that turned out some 200 vessels.

The captains' wealth built the town's distinctive mansions — arched windows, marble fireplaces, exotic art brought home from round-the-world voyages, and a widow's walk on the roof where a family could watch the horizon for a returning sail. In Searsport specifically, it's said about half the captains' wives went to sea with their husbands rather than wait ashore, sometimes bearing and raising children at sea. The Penobscot Marine Museum in the middle of town keeps that history now; Searsport still calls itself Maine's Antique Capital, a quieter legacy of the wealth that maritime trade once brought through here.
properties.source: Penobscot Marine Museum; Wikipedia — Searsport, Maine and Searsport Historic District

properties.title: From cargo schooners to the Windjammer Capital of the World
properties.body:
By the 1930s, the working schooners that had carried granite, lime, and lumber up and down this coast for a century were being retired wholesale — replaced by trucks, rail, and steel-hulled steamers. A Maine mariner named Captain Frank Swift had a different idea: buy the old vessels as they came off cargo duty, fit them out for passengers, and sell pleasure cruises instead of scrapping them. His first cruise sailed in 1936 aboard a 55-year-old schooner named Mabel. By 1938 he had three vessels and a Life magazine cover story; by 1940 he had five, and Camden had earned the nickname 'Windjammer Capital of the World.'

The idea outlived its founder. By 1977 there were enough separate schooner businesses operating out of Camden and Rockland that they formed the Maine Windjammer Association to market together, and it's still sailing today — a working fleet, several vessels designated National Historic Landmarks, some hulls dating back to the 1800s, carrying passengers instead of cargo along the same routes their captains once sailed for a living. It's the clearest through-line between the bay's 19th-century working-sail economy and the one that supports it now.
properties.source: Maine Windjammer Association; Frommer's — The Maine Windjammers: 75 Years Young

properties.title: Pond Island (Brooksville)

islandInfo.ownership: Maine Coast Heritage Trust (transferred from Philadelphia Conservationists, Inc. in 1995)
islandInfo.publicAccess: Day use and camping at 3 established campsites (2-night limit); groups of 6+ and commercial use restricted to a permit-only site on the pond's eastern edge
islandInfo.notes: 32 acres near the western end of Eggemoggin Reach. Reach by boat from the Castine town dock or the Bridge End boat launch on Deer Isle. Town dock floats available May 15–Oct 15. Pets must be kept under control; stay on established trails.

properties.title: Battle Island (Penobscot)

islandInfo.ownership: Maine Coast Heritage Trust (bargain sale in 2011, with support from the Maine Island Trail Association)
islandInfo.publicAccess: Day use and camping at one established campsite (2-night limit); groups of 6+ and commercial use by permit only; no campfires; carry out all trash
islandInfo.notes: Two-acre island rising from the Bagaduce River; connects to the mainland and MCHT's adjoining Till's Point Preserve via mudflats at low tide. Boat access only — land via the staircase on the island's south side. Nearest public launch: Winslow Cove, Penobscot village, just under 2 miles.

properties.source: Maine Coast Heritage Trust — Battle Island preserve page (mcht.org)

properties.title: Sheep Island (Owls Head)

islandInfo.ownership: Maine Coast Heritage Trust (acquired December 2021)
islandInfo.publicAccess: Day use and camping at one established campsite (2-night limit, first-come first-served)
islandInfo.notes: 76 undeveloped acres in West Penobscot Bay. Land on the cobble beach on the north shore — watch for a submerged bar just north of it at low tide. Reach from the Mechanic Street public launch in Rockland (~4 miles) or Richard Carver Harbor Park in Owls Head (~1 mile, hand-carried boats only); overnight parking needs a free permit from the Owls Head town office.

properties.source: Maine Coast Heritage Trust — Sheep Island preserve page (mcht.org)

properties.title: Monroe Island (Owls Head)

islandInfo.ownership: Maine Coast Heritage Trust (bought from the Faunce family in 2018)
islandInfo.publicAccess: Day use and camping at established campsites (2-night limit); groups of 6+ need a permit
islandInfo.notes: 225 acres — one of the largest undeveloped islands on the midcoast, with a 2-mile trail network. Approach from the west side, where six beaches allow safe landing (the float and ramp are currently closed). Reach from Rockland (~4 miles) or Owls Head (~0.5 miles, hand-carried boats only); overnight parking needs a free permit from the Owls Head town office.

properties.source: Maine Coast Heritage Trust — Monroe Island, Owls Head preserve page (mcht.org)

properties.title: Hurricane Island (Vinalhaven)

islandInfo.ownership: Privately owned by the Gaston family; leased since 2010 to the nonprofit Hurricane Island Foundation under a 40-year lease
islandInfo.publicAccess: Operated as a research and education field station (Hurricane Island Center for Science and Leadership); a Maine Island Trail Association campsite is maintained on the island's north end for MITA members
islandInfo.notes: A former granite-quarry company town (see the History entry for this island). Ownership stayed private — this isn't a land-trust acquisition — but the long-term lease to a nonprofit operator makes access genuinely public in practice.

properties.source: Hurricane Island Center for Science and Leadership (hurricaneisland.net); Wikipedia — Hurricane Island (Maine)

properties.title: Isle au Haut

islandInfo.ownership: Split ownership: roughly half the island is Acadia National Park, donated to the federal government in 1943 by heirs of the island's founding family; the other half is private land, home to the year-round fishing community and summer residents
islandInfo.publicAccess: The Acadia National Park half (Duck Harbor area) is open to hikers and permitted campers; the private half is not — the town/park boundary is not always obvious from the water
islandInfo.notes: A working town (year-round population 92 per the 2020 Census — see the Demographics entry) shares this island with a genuinely separate unit of Acadia National Park; the two halves have different rules.

properties.source: Acadia National Park / NPS — Isle au Haut Boundary Law (nps.gov/acad); Wikipedia — Isle au Haut, Maine

properties.title: Clark Island (St. George)

properties.source: Maine Coast Heritage Trust — Clark Island preserve page (mcht.org); Portland Press Herald, "Purchase protects Clark Island preserve in the midcoast" (2020)

properties.title: The fishing village that filled Pulpit Harbor
properties.body:
People owned land around Pulpit Harbor as early as 1764, but the village didn't reach its peak until the second half of the nineteenth century, when it was the commercial, religious, and social center of North Haven. An 1898 Rockland Courier-Gazette reporter counted 25 or 30 houses scattered along the shore, with farms behind producing butter, eggs, and berries for local tables. At its height the harbor held two fish processing plants, four mills, a post office, five stores, boat shops, and a school — Roscoe Babbidge's store stood where the town landing sits today, and fishermen traded dried fish there for rum brought up from the Caribbean. A dozen or so two-masted mackerel schooners worked out of the harbor at the fishery's peak.

The decline set in around 1900. The mackerel fishery dropped off sharply, and steam power was replacing sail up and down the coast — Pulpit Harbor's deep, protected water had been valuable specifically because it suited sailing vessels, and that advantage mattered less once steamships could pass safely through the Thoroughfare instead. The sawmill and gristmill at the head of Mill Stream closed, the wood trade that had supplied the mainland lime kilns ceased, and families began moving away or relocating to the Thoroughfare village. Hanson Crockett's store housed the Pulpit Harbor post office starting in 1903, with his wife Meribah serving as postmaster until it finally closed in 1932 — by then most of the old farmland around the harbor had passed to summer residents.
properties.source: North Haven Historical Society — "Pulpit Harbor: The Old Village" (northhavenmainehistoricalsociety.org)

properties.title: How a lime-quarrying boom built Rockland Harbor
properties.body:
Rockland didn't start with that name. European settlers first called this stretch of shore Lermond's Cove, after John Lermond and his brothers, who set up a lumber operation here in 1767; it became known as Shore Village when Thomaston was incorporated in 1777, then East Thomaston when it was set off as its own town in 1848. The town took the name Rockland in 1850, a direct nod to the limestone cliffs that were about to define its economy for the next century.

Limestone quarried from the hills behind town was burned into lime in kilns lined up along the harbor itself, then shipped out in watertight casks to build the mortar and plaster of cities up and down the East Coast. By 1854 Rockland was operating twelve quarries and 125 lime kilns and had become the country's leading lime producer; by 1886 the industry employed over a thousand workers and more than 300 vessels carried the lime to market. Shipbuilding grew up right alongside it — in 1854 alone Rockland's yards launched eleven ships, three barks, six brigs, and four schooners. Between 1881 and 1900 the Army Corps of Engineers built the Rockland Breakwater specifically to protect this harbor and the industry crowded around it, a nearly mile-long stone arm that still reaches out into the bay today.

The lime industry that built the harbor didn't disappear overnight, but it did eventually run its course: the last of Rockland's kilns went dark in 1958.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Rockland, Maine

properties.title: Three thousand years of camps on Eggemoggin Reach
properties.body:
Archaeological digs at Scott's Landing in 2007-2008 uncovered a shell midden with seasonal encampments dating back 3,000 to 2,500 years — the oldest layers holding spear points and stone scraping tools, the middle layers showing roughly 2,000 years of intermittent seasonal use, and the uppermost layers turning up 16th- and 17th-century European trade goods: glass beads, clay pipe fragments, worked metal.

The people early French and English visitors recorded here as "Etchemins" — a term used for certain Wabanaki communities of the Maine coast — built fishing weirs across Eggemoggin Reach between Deer Isle and Little Deer Isle to spear flounder as the tide turned, a technique English settlers later adopted themselves. The name Eggemoggin itself is Wabanaki, usually translated as "fish-weir place" or "place where the current runs both ways" — apt for a reach where the tide reverses direction as it drains two different bays. Long before Deer Isle had a European name, this was already a working, fished, and camped-on shore, generation after generation.
properties.source: Maine by Foot — Scott's Landing, Deer Isle; Island Institute — More Than a Pile of Shells

properties.title: Deer on every shore, then a town called Deer Isle
properties.body:
English colonists named these islands for the deer that once crowded their shores in the 1600s and 1700s, long before anyone lived here year-round. The first permanent settler, William Eaton, arrived in 1762 and built near what became known as the Scott Farm; the first English child born on the island, Timothy Billings, followed in May 1764, and the first church went up in 1773.

Incorporated as a town on February 2, 1789, Deer Isle originally stretched across three islands now split into separate towns: Little Deer Isle, Deer Isle proper, and Isle au Haut. Isle au Haut broke away in 1874; a little over a century after incorporation, the granite boom split off the island's southern third as well, forming the town of Stonington in 1897 — itself known simply as "Green's Landing" until that name change. What's now three separate towns on the chart was, within living memory of its own founding, all one.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Deer Isle, Maine; Genealogy Trails — History of Deer Isle

properties.title: Why they call it Merchant Row
properties.body:
Every island-studded passage needs a name, and this one takes its name from a person, not a trade: Nathaniel Merchant, an early landowner who grew up on the island that still carries his family name today. The row of islands beyond it — McGlathery, Round, Devil, Spectacle, Hell's Half Acre, and dozens more — inherited the surname as a group identity for the whole archipelago between Stonington and Isle au Haut.

The islands were inhabited and worked long before any Merchant arrived: a shell midden on the southeast end of nearby Nathan Island shows Native use spanning the Ceramic Period, roughly 3,000 to 500 years ago — a second, separate site from the better-documented one at Scott's Landing on Deer Isle, evidence that this whole archipelago, not just its larger islands, was part of a long-inhabited coastal landscape well before European settlement, land grants, or the family name that stuck.
properties.source: Maine Coast Heritage Trust — History of Merchant Row

properties.title: The High Island, named in passing by Champlain
properties.body:
Samuel de Champlain named this island in 1604 during the same coasting voyage that brought him into Penobscot Bay — Isle au Haut, "high island," for the way its hills rise above every other island around it, visible from well out to sea. It stayed largely unsettled for nearly two centuries after that; farmers, fishermen, and boatbuilders began arriving in earnest only after the Revolution, with a small summer colony taking root in the 1880s once city visitors discovered it.

Isle au Haut split off from Deer Isle to incorporate as its own town in 1874. Its French name never changed even as everything around it did — mariners and mapmakers alike kept Champlain's word for it, one of the few Penobscot Bay place names from that first summer of contact still in everyday use, spoken by lobstermen radioing each other today exactly as a French explorer wrote it down four centuries ago.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Isle au Haut, Maine; Ellsworth American — Away we go to Isle au Haut

properties.title: Maine's last working granite quarry
properties.body:
Job L. Goss began quarrying granite on Crotch Island in 1869; his son John L. Goss took over in 1887 and built the operation into the John L. Goss Corporation, which acquired the neighboring F.S. Warren quarry in 1896 and began working Moose Island by the late 1890s. At its peak around 1905, roughly 80 men worked Crotch Island and another 100 worked Moose Island; the main Goss Quarry, opened in 1872, had grown to 350 feet square and 120 feet deep.

Crotch Island's distinctive pink-tinted stone — sold as "Sherwood pink" and "Goss pink" — went into the approaches of the Brooklyn Bridge and the piers of the Blackwell's Island Bridge over New York's East River (today's Roosevelt Island Bridge), carried south from this one small island by schooner. Like Hurricane Island's quarry, the workforce was heavily immigrant — Swedish, Italian, Scottish, and Finnish stonecutters among them. Reinforced concrete ended most of Maine's island quarrying by the 1920s and 30s; Goss himself died in 1936, and the company changed hands in 1953. Crotch Island's quarry alone survived — closed in 1966, revived in 1979, and still cutting granite today, the last one operating on a Maine island.
properties.source: Island Institute — Stonington's Past Carved in Granite; Quarries and Beyond — Maine Granite Quarry List; Deer Isle Granite Museum

properties.title: A granite boomtown outgrows its old name
properties.body:
Granite quarrying took off on Deer Isle's southern peninsula around 1870, and within thirty years it had remade the place completely. The waterfront village of Green's Landing swelled toward 4,000 residents by 1900 — quarries running on Green Island (the Russ Stone Quarry, opened 1881), Crotch Island (Goss & Small, from 1889), and beyond, shipping stone to New York and Boston for bridges, banks, and government buildings. By the 1910 census, quarrymen actually outnumbered fishermen here, a startling reversal for a town that had always lived by the sea in the other sense. Local tradition holds that some of the last granite cut on these islands ended up as curbstones on New York's Fifth Avenue.

The boom was big enough, and different enough from farming, fishing Deer Isle to the north, that the Maine Legislature let the southern third break away as its own town on February 18, 1897 — renamed Stonington, for the industry that built it, replacing the working name Green's Landing had carried for generations.
properties.source: Maine: An Encyclopedia — Deer Isle; Town of Stonington — History; Wikipedia — Stonington, Maine

properties.title: From cod and mackerel to a lobster economy
properties.body:
For most of the 19th century, cod and mackerel were the backbone of the fishery here, not lobster — canneries at Burnt Cove and at Green's Landing packed mackerel and clams for shipment, part of a regional network that ran 23 lobster canneries by 1880, absorbing roughly two-thirds of the whole Maine catch for Boston and New York markets. Lobster only became the dominant catch later, as overfishing and shifting markets hit the old groundfish stocks hard in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

The timing lined up with another local collapse: as granite quarrying wound down through the early 1900s, out-of-work quarrymen turned to lobstering to make a living, feeding people and boats into the same waters at the same moment groundfish were declining and lobster demand was rising. That double transition — from cod to lobster, and from stonecutters to lobstermen — is the direct ancestor of the harbor sailors pass through Stonington today, long since Maine's single largest lobster port by value.
properties.source: Town of Stonington — History; Downeast Fisheries Trail — Lobster; Wild Maine — Stonington Lobster Economy

properties.title: How Merchant Row became a conservation landscape
properties.body:
McGlathery Island has one of the longest conservation histories of any Maine island — a Canadian nonprofit called Friends of Nature bought it in 1954, decades before land trusts were common, and held it as an unusually early example of private island conservation before finally transferring it to Maine Coast Heritage Trust in 2021.

MCHT has since built out an eleven-preserve network across the wider archipelago: Green Island (47 acres, donated 1993), Saddleback Island (76 acres, purchased 2004), Nathan and Little Nathan Islands (2001), Bill's Island (an estate gift in 2005), The Fort (2001-2005), Sand Island and Eastern Mark Island (2003-2004), plus Gooseberry, Little Camp, and Andrews Islands added as recently as 2016. Roughly two-thirds of Merchant Row's fifty-some islands are protected today, built up piece by piece over five decades by multiple landowners and organizations rather than any single acquisition — a working example of how an entire named passage, not just one island at a time, can end up conserved.
properties.source: Maine Coast Heritage Trust — History of Merchant Row; Ellsworth American — Maine Coast Heritage Trust Protects Islands Along Merchant Row

properties.title: A gift Isle au Haut didn't entirely want
properties.body:
Ernest Bowditch — grandson of the navigator Nathaniel Bowditch, whose navigation manual still guides sailors two centuries later — built a summer resort called the Point Lookout Club on Isle au Haut and bought up large tracts of the island around it. Acadia National Park's backers first asked him to donate land around World War I; he said no.

It was his heirs, led by Richard Bowditch, who wrote to Interior Secretary Harold Ickes on July 6, 1942, proposing the gift Ernest never made — roughly 3,000 acres across the island's southern half, accepted in 1943 and formalized in January 1944. The gift wasn't universally welcomed on the island itself: some year-round residents opposed losing tax base and local control over land their town had always governed alone. Isle au Haut still runs that way today — the town governs most of the island, the Park Service manages only the donated southern portion — an unusually split arrangement for Acadia, and a reminder that "national park" and "island community" aren't always the same wish.
properties.source: National Park Service — Isle au Haut history; Isle au Haut Community Oral History; Island Institute — Acadia's Offshore Island

properties.title: The small island town that outlands every other port in Maine
properties.body:
Stonington has been Maine's top lobster port by landed value for years running, not by a small margin — $46.3 million and roughly 15 million pounds in 2011 (its fourth straight year at #1), climbing to $60 million by 2014 and a record $77.3 million in 2021 before settling back to $44.7 million in 2022, still enough to hold the top spot. In 2025 the harbor landed roughly $49 million, about 22 percent of the combined value of Maine's ten busiest ports put together.

One town's fleet outproducing every other harbor in the state, working the same waters its quarrymen-turned-lobstermen first worked a century ago. It's easy to miss from the water, threading between working boats stacked three deep at the co-op floats, just how much of the state's whole lobster economy funnels through this one small harbor.
properties.source: Ellsworth American — Stonington is Maine's Top Lobster Port Once Again; Island Institute — Stonington Tops in Lobster Again, Hitting $60 Million Mark; Rising Tide — Lobster Landings 2025

properties.title: The bridge with the same flaw as Tacoma Narrows — fixed in time
properties.body:
Before 1939, the only way onto Deer Isle from the mainland was a ferry across Eggemoggin Reach, which locals had come to consider antiquated and dangerous. The WPA-funded suspension bridge that replaced it, dedicated June 19, 1939, was designed by Holton D. Robinson and David B. Steinman — and it shared a design flaw with a much more famous bridge: a stiffening girder too shallow for its span, prone to oscillating in the wind, the same flaw that brought down the original Tacoma Narrows Bridge in November 1940.

Deer Isle's bridge never collapsed, but after watching newsreel footage of Tacoma Narrows twisting itself apart, Steinman came back to Eggemoggin Reach himself and retrofitted his own bridge with extra cable and floor stays to stiffen it against exactly that failure. It has carried traffic safely ever since — a bridge that could have been a second famous collapse, saved by its own engineer learning from the first one in time.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Deer Isle Bridge; Island Institute — The Year Steel and Cable Changed Deer Isle; Living New Deal; HistoricBridges.org
